guides.intro: A fire needs all three material stages ready before you strike anything: tinder that catches a spark, kindling that catches tinder, and fuel that holds the burn. Gather triple what looks sufficient.

items.title: Tepee
items.blurb: Kindling leaned into a cone over the tinder. Lights easiest and burns hot and fast, so it is the starting lay: collapse it into coals, then feed a steadier lay from them.

tools.label: Ask about this
tools.question: My tepee fire keeps collapsing before it catches. What am I doing wrong?

items.title: Log cabin
items.blurb: Fuel stacked in alternating pairs around the flame. Airflow through the walls gives a long, steady burn for cooking and warmth once the tepee has caught.

items.title: Spark ignition
items.blurb: A ferro rod or flint against steel throws sparks into prepared tinder: shaved bark, dry grass, or cotton teased into a loose nest. Shave the rod slowly first to load the nest with material.

items.title: Site preparation
items.blurb: Clear ground to mineral soil in a two-meter circle, and build a platform of green wood on wet ground. Wind decides placement: shelter the flame, and never lay a fire under snow-loaded branches.

tools.label: Ask about this
tools.question: Where should I place a fire relative to my shelter and the wind?

guides.intro: Rope work turns loose materials into shelters, tools, and anchors. Learn six knots well rather than twenty badly: each one below states its job, and the camera can check your result against it.

items.title: Bowline
items.blurb: A fixed loop that will not slip under load and unties easily afterward. Use it to anchor a line around a tree or your waist. The loop stays the size you tie it.

tools.label: Ask about this
tools.question: When do I use a bowline instead of a figure-eight loop?

items.title: Taut-line hitch
items.blurb: An adjustable hitch that slides to tension a line and then holds. Use it on tent guy-lines and any line you will need to re-tighten as it stretches.

items.title: Clove hitch
items.blurb: Two crossing turns around a pole. Fast to tie and to adjust, and the usual start and end of a lashing. It slips on a smooth pole under a shifting pull, so back it up when the load moves.

items.title: Trucker's hitch
items.blurb: A loop plus a pulley wrap that multiplies your pull for cinching a load tight. Use it to bind bundles or strain a ridgeline before locking it off with half hitches.

items.title: Figure-eight
items.blurb: A stopper that keeps a rope end from pulling through a hole or another knot, and the base of the figure-eight loop. Bulkier and stronger than an overhand.

items.title: Square knot
items.blurb: Joins two ends of the same rope around an object, such as a bandage or a bundle. It is a binding knot: never trust it to join two ropes under load.

items.title: Square lashing
items.blurb: Binds two poles at a right angle: start with a clove hitch, wrap three turns over and under, frap two turns between the poles, and finish with a clove hitch. The frame joint for shelters and racks.

items.title: Shear lashing
items.blurb: Binds two poles side by side so they scissor open into an A-frame. Wrap loosely enough that the legs still spread, then frap between the poles.

items.title: Plant fibers
items.blurb: Inner bark of dead standing trees, dried nettle or milkweed stalks, and yucca leaves all strip into usable fiber. Test a strand: it should bend around itself without snapping.

items.title: Reverse-wrap twist
items.blurb: Twist a fiber bundle away from you until it kinks, fold it, then twist each half away while wrapping them toward each other. Splice in new fiber before a strand thins out.

guides.intro: Most mushroom poisonings follow a confident wrong identification. Chapter 10's rule: identify to species on structural features before anything touches your mouth. Folk tests fail here; color, taste, and tarnished spoons detect nothing.

items.title: Mushroom identification
items.blurb: Troubleshoot the likely species of this mushroom based on the shape of the mushroom cap, gills, and stem.
